Section 4 – Treatment Works and Capacity

4.1 General

This section describes the principal treatment works operated by the Authority and the design parameters that govern their operation. It is intended as a reference for operational staff, maintenance planners, and engineers engaged in capital works. Where a particular parameter is subject to review, the review status is noted against the entry. All design figures quoted in this section are taken from the latest revision of the relevant process design memorandum, unless otherwise stated.

4.2 Eastgate Treatment Works (ENT02)

4.2.1 Location and Role

Eastgate Treatment Works is situated on the eastern edge of Thornwick, adjacent to the Eastgate Pumping Station and the main trunk road. The works receives raw water from the Eastgate Reservoir via a 600 mm diameter inlet main, and from the River Corby via the Corby Intake, which is approximately 1.2 km upstream of the works. The works provides the majority of the potable supply for District North and provides a top-up supply to District East during periods of high demand.

4.2.2 Design Capacity

Eastgate Treatment Works design capacity 45000 cubic metres per day. Record status: current. This figure is the current design capacity and is the basis for all hydraulic and process calculations within this manual. It represents the maximum sustainable output of the works under normal raw water quality conditions, with all process streams in service and no unit out of service for maintenance.

The design capacity is subject to annual review by the Engineering Planning Group. Any proposed change to the design capacity must be supported by a process modelling assessment and approved by the Head of Water Treatment before being incorporated into a future revision of this manual.

4.2.3 Process Description

The treatment process at Eastgate comprises the following principal stages, in order:

- Screening and grit removal (2 no. duty screens, 1 no. standby)
- Coagulation and flocculation (3 no. flocculation tanks, each with 2 no. stages)
- Clarification (4 no. lamella clarifiers)
- Rapid gravity filtration (8 no. filter beds, each with a nominal area of 45 m²)
- Chlorination (primary and secondary disinfection)
- pH correction and fluoridation
- Treated water storage (2 no. contact tanks, total capacity 12,500 m³)

The works operates as a conventional surface water treatment plant. The coagulation process uses ferric sulphate, with pH adjustment by lime. Polyelectrolyte is dosed as a flocculant aid. The normal coagulant dose range is 25–45 mg/l, depending on raw water turbidity and colour.

4.2.4 Flow Splitting and Control

Inlet flow is split equally between the three flocculation tanks by means of flow control valves on the inlet header. Each flocculation tank is fitted with a magnetic flow meter, and the flow set points are controlled by the works SCADA system. The normal operating range for each tank is 0.45–0.65 m³/s.

Clarified water from the lamella clarifiers is collected in a common clarified water channel, from which it is drawn by gravity to the filter inlet distribution chamber. The filter inlet is controlled by individual inlet valves, which are trimmed to give an equal flow to each filter bed. The normal filtration rate is 4.5–5.5 m/h, with a maximum rate of 6.0 m/h for short periods during filter backwash.

4.2.5 Filter Operation

Each rapid gravity filter bed is of the conventional downflow type, with a dual media of anthracite over sand, supported on a gravel layer and a nozzle floor. The normal filter run length is between 24 and 48 hours, depending on raw water quality. The end of a filter run is determined by the head loss across the bed, which is monitored continuously. The terminal head loss is normally 2.0 m, but this may be reduced to 1.5 m during periods of high algal activity in the raw water.

### 1. INTRODUCTION

#### 1.1 Purpose of this Manual

This manual sets out the approved methods, safety protocols, and performance standards for the operation and maintenance of the Thornwick Water Authority surface water treatment works. It is intended for use by all technicians, engineers, and operators engaged in the day-to-day running of the plant.

#### 1.2 Organisational Structure and Responsibilities

The treatment works operates under the overall management of the Operations Manager, who is responsible for the safe and efficient delivery of treated water to the distribution network. The operational team is structured as follows:

**Operations Manager** – Overall responsibility for plant performance, compliance with regulatory standards, staff management, and the annual review of this manual. The current Operations Manager is **Clarissa Finch**, who has held the post since **1 April 2019**. Clarissa Finch start date 2019-04-01 date. Record status: current. All significant operational decisions, emergency interventions, and deviations from standard procedures must be referred to the Operations Manager or, in their absence, to the Deputy Operations Manager.

**Deputy Operations Manager** – Supports the Operations Manager in the day-to-day running of the plant and assumes full responsibility in the absence of the Operations Manager. The post is currently held by **Dennis Okafor**. Responsibilities include shift rota management, coordination of maintenance activities with the workshop team, and the preparation of monthly performance reports.

**Senior Process Technician (Shift Leader)** – Each shift is led by a Senior Process Technician who directs the work of the process technicians on that shift. Shift Leaders are responsible for monitoring plant parameters, responding to alarms, and carrying out routine process checks. They report directly to the Deputy Operations Manager.

**Process Technicians** – Carry out routine operational duties including plant inspections, water quality sampling, filter backwashing, chemical dosing checks, and minor maintenance tasks. Process Technicians work on a rotating shift pattern covering 24 hours per day, 365 days per year.

**Maintenance Technicians (Mechanical and Electrical)** – Responsible for planned and reactive maintenance of all plant and equipment. Mechanical and electrical disciplines are separate, and each has its own supervisor. Maintenance activities are coordinated through the Works Maintenance Planner, who works closely with the Deputy Operations Manager.

**Water Quality Technicians** – Based in the on-site laboratory, they carry out the routine sampling and analysis programme. They also support the process team in investigating any water quality excursions and are responsible for the calibration of online analysers.

**Administrative Support** – The works office provides administrative support to the operations team, including the management of records, purchasing, and the coordination of training.

Section 1.5 Environmental Compliance and Permit Obligations

1.5.1 General Requirements

This Section sets out the environmental compliance requirements that apply to the operation and maintenance of Thornwick Water Authority (TWA) assets. All personnel involved in maintenance activities shall be familiar with the relevant permit conditions and shall conduct their work in a manner that prevents pollution and minimises environmental impact.

The principal environmental permit for TWA operations is held with the Environment Agency. The Environment Agency issued permit number WA-2018-0456. Record status: current. This permit is current and shall remain in force until such time as it is varied, transferred, or revoked by the Environment Agency. A copy of the permit and its associated conditions is held in the Environmental Compliance file in the Administrative Support office, and an electronic copy is available on the shared drive under TWA/Environmental/Permits.

1.5.2 Permit Conditions Summary

The following conditions are those most relevant to maintenance activities. This summary is not exhaustive. Where a conflict arises between this summary and the permit itself, the permit conditions shall take precedence.

- Discharges to watercourses shall not cause an obvious film, sheen, or discolouration on the surface of the water, nor cause the deposition of solids on the bed of the watercourse.
- Chemical storage areas shall be bunded to 110% of the capacity of the largest stored container, and all bunds shall be maintained free of accumulated rainwater and debris.
- Spill kits shall be available at all locations where oils, fuels, or chemicals are stored or used, and shall be checked monthly.
- Any incident that causes or has the potential to cause pollution shall be reported to the Environment Agency as soon as practicable, and in any event within 24 hours of the incident being detected.
- Maintenance activities that involve the use of concrete, cement, or grout shall be carried out in such a way as to prevent the entry of these materials into any drain or watercourse.

1.5.3 Reporting Obligations

The following reporting obligations apply to TWA under the permit:

- Annual environmental performance report, submitted to the Environment Agency by 31 January each year, covering the preceding calendar year.
- Quarterly notification of any permit breaches, submitted within 14 days of the end of each calendar quarter.
- Immediate notification by telephone of any incident that causes significant pollution, followed by a written report within 24 hours.

The Works Environmental Officer is responsible for preparing and submitting all reports required by the permit. In the absence of the Works Environmental Officer, the Operations Manager shall assume this responsibility.

1.5.4 Environmental Risk Assessment for Maintenance Activities

Before commencing any maintenance activity that could have an environmental impact, a site-specific environmental risk assessment shall be completed using Form TW/ERA/02. The risk assessment shall identify:

- The potential pathways by which pollutants could reach the environment;
- The likelihood and severity of any potential pollution event;
- The control measures required to prevent pollution;
- The spill response arrangements in place.

The completed form shall be kept with the work permit or work instruction for the activity, and shall be reviewed by the person in charge of the work before work commences.

1.5.5 Oil and Fuel Storage

All oil and fuel storage tanks on TWA sites shall be inspected weekly for signs of leakage, corrosion, or damage. The results of these inspections shall be recorded in the site log.

**1.7.6 Firmware Update Procedure**

Firmware updates to SCADA components shall be carried out in accordance with the change control procedure (Section 1.9). The following steps shall be followed:

1. Obtain the firmware update package from the equipment manufacturer or the IT Systems Manager.
2. Verify the integrity of the update package using the checksum provided by the manufacturer.
3. Back up the current configuration and database of the device to be updated.
4. Schedule the update during a planned outage or maintenance window. Updates to the primary server shall be carried out during a period of low operational demand, and shall be coordinated with the shift manager.
5. Apply the firmware update to the standby unit first. Verify that the standby unit operates correctly and can synchronise with the primary unit.
6. Once the standby unit is confirmed operational, apply the update to the primary unit.
7. After the update is complete, verify the system functionality, including alarm annunciation, data logging, and operator displays.
8. Record the update in the SCADA System Change Log, including the date, component, previous and new firmware versions, and the name of the person carrying out the update.

The current firmware status of the SCADA System is recorded in the SCADA System Configuration Register, held by the IT Systems Manager. The register shall be updated within one working day of any firmware change.

Quarterly, a communication path test shall be carried out on all RTUs. Each RTU shall be disconnected from the main communications network, and the fallback path shall be tested. RTUs that fail the test shall be reported to the IT Systems Manager.

**1.8 Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) Procedure**

**1.8.1 Purpose**

This procedure establishes the minimum requirements for the locking out and tagging of energy isolating devices whenever maintenance or servicing is carried out on plant or equipment where the unexpected energisation, start-up or release of stored energy could cause injury. All persons carrying out such work shall comply with this procedure. No person shall attempt to operate any switch, valve or other energy isolating device that has been locked or tagged out.

**1.8.2 Definitions**

For the purpose of this procedure:

- *Affected person* – a person whose work requires them to operate, or be in the vicinity of, equipment that is being serviced or maintained under a LOTO.
- *Authorised person* – a person who has been trained and authorised to carry out LOTO and to perform the servicing or maintenance.
- *Energy isolating device* – a mechanical device that physically prevents the transmission or release of energy, including manually operated circuit breakers, disconnect switches, line valves, and blocks.
- *Lockout* – the placement of a lock and tag on an energy isolating device in accordance with an established procedure, ensuring that the device cannot be operated until the lock is removed.
- *Tagout* – the placement of a tag on an energy isolating device in accordance with an established procedure, to indicate that the device may not be operated until the tag is removed. Tagout shall only be used where a device is not capable of being locked out, and shall always be used in conjunction with an additional safety measure, such as the removal of a fuse or the disconnection of a pipe.

**1.8.3 General Requirements**

1. LOTO shall be used whenever servicing or maintenance is carried out on plant or equipment that could be inadvertently energised, started, or release stored energy. This includes, but is not limited to, work on pumps, valves, actuators, chemical dosing systems, and electrical switchgear.
2. Only authorised persons shall carry out LOTO. A current list of authorised persons is held by the Operations Manager and displayed on the notice board at each depot.
3. Each authorised person shall be issued with a personal lock and key. Personal locks shall be uniquely keyed and shall only be operated by the person to whom they are issued. Keys shall not be duplicated or loaned.
4. Where more than one person is working on the same equipment, each person shall attach their own personal lock to the energy isolating device, or to a multi-lock hasp fitted to that device.
5. Locks and tags shall be of a robust construction and shall be capable of remaining in place for the duration of the work. Tags shall be weatherproof and shall be attached with a non-reusable cable tie or other secure fixing.
6. Tags shall be filled in legibly with a ballpoint pen or permanent marker, stating the reason for the lockout, the date, and the name of the authorised person. Do not use pencil or any other erasable medium.

When the servicing or maintenance is complete, the following steps shall be carried out:

| Check gland leakage; adjust or repack as necessary | W | 9.3.1 |
| Check bearing housing temperature by hand; record any reading above 70°C | W | 9.3.2 |
| Check for unusual noise or vibration | W | 9.3.3 |
| Check coupling alignment using straight edge and feeler gauge | Q | 9.3.4 |
| Lubricate bearings (grease) – see Section 9.8 | Q | 9.8.2 |
| Check and tighten foundation bolts | SA | 9.3.5 |
| Check flexible coupling elements for wear; replace if cracked or perished | SA | 9.3.6 |
| Inspect impeller and wear rings; measure clearances and record | A | 9.3.7 |
| Check shaft run-out at coupling and at gland | A | 9.3.8 |
| Megger test motor windings (in conjunction with electrical section) | A | 9.3.9 |
| Overhaul – replace bearings, mechanical seal or gland packing, and inspect all internal surfaces | 20,000 h | 9.3.10 |

**9.3.1 Gland Leakage**

For packed glands, the acceptable leakage rate is a steady drip of between 10 and 30 drops per minute when the pump is running at its duty point. A dry gland indicates that the packing is too tight, which will cause scoring of the shaft sleeve. A stream of water indicates that the packing is too loose or is worn. Adjust the gland nuts by a quarter turn at a time and re-check after 15 minutes of running.

For mechanical seals, there should be no visible leakage. A small amount of weeping may occur during the initial run-in period of a new seal and is acceptable for the first 4 hours of operation. Thereafter, any leakage is a fault and the seal shall be replaced.

**9.3.2 Bearing Housing Temperature**

The bearing housing temperature shall be checked by hand. If the housing is too hot to hold the back of a hand against for more than 3 seconds, the temperature is likely to be above 70°C and the pump shall be taken out of service for investigation. The pump shall not be returned to service until the cause of the overheating has been identified and rectified. Record the temperature and the action taken on the job card.
**Thornwick Water Authority Maintenance Manual**

**Section 9.4 – Routine Inspection of Horizontal Split-Case Pumps**

The checks in this section apply to the horizontal split-case pumps installed at Crowthorne Hill Pumping Station (CHPS), Merrow Lane Booster (MLB), and the Low Lift station at Ashcombe Works. They supplement the general pump checks in Section 9.3 and are to be carried out in accordance with the frequency table below.

| Item | Frequency | Ref. |
|---|---|---|
| Check suction and discharge pressure gauges for erratic readings | W | 9.4.1 |
| Inspect coupling guard for security and correct alignment | W | 9.4.2 |
| Check drain valve at bottom of casing is closed and not weeping | W | 9.4.3 |
| Check casing joint for signs of leakage; note any seepage on job card | W | 9.4.4 |
| Verify pressure switch settings against pump curve for the current duty | M | 9.4.5 |
| Check air release valve operation on the discharge header | M | 9.4.6 |
| Inspect baseplate and grout for cracks or fretting | SA | 9.4.7 |
| Check shaft sleeve condition at gland area; measure and record wear | A | 9.4.8 |
| Dismantle and inspect non-return valve on discharge; renew if flap worn | A | 9.4.9 |

**9.4.1 Pressure Gauge Readings**

Erratic gauge readings usually indicate air entrainment or a partially blocked suction strainer. If the suction gauge shows a vacuum higher than the value on the duty card, stop the pump and check the strainer. Do not attempt to clear a blocked strainer by throttling the discharge valve. Record the readings on the daily log sheet at CHPS. At MLB, where the suction head is positive, a sudden drop in suction pressure may indicate a fault with the town’s inlet main; contact the Network Controller before taking the pump out of service.

**9.4.2 Coupling Guard**

The guard shall be in place at all times when the pump is running. Check that all fixing bolts are present and that the guard does not rub on the coupling. If the guard has been removed for maintenance, it shall be replaced before the pump is returned to service. A missing guard is a reportable safety defect and shall be entered on the safety observation register.

**9.4.3 Casing Drain Valve**

The drain valve at the bottom of the casing shall be closed except when the pump is being drained. If the valve is found weeping, tighten the gland nut. If weeping continues, replace the valve. Do not leave a bucket under the valve as a permanent arrangement; this is not an acceptable long-term fix.

**9.4.4 Casing Joint Leakage**

A small amount of seepage at the casing joint can occur on older pumps and is not necessarily a fault. Wipe the joint clean and monitor. If the seepage increases or becomes a steady drip, the joint shall be re-sealed at the next available outage. For CHPS Pump 1, a previous seepage at the top half of the casing was traced to a distorted joint face. That pump is booked for a full overhaul in the current financial year and the joint faces will be machined true at that time.

**9.4.5 Pressure Switch Settings**

Pressure switch settings shall be checked against the current duty card for the pump. The duty card is held in the pump house at CHPS and in the kiosk at MLB. Settings shall be verified using a calibrated test gauge. Do not adjust settings without reference to the duty card. If a setting is found to be outside the permitted band, record the discrepancy on the job card and notify the Mechanical Engineer.

**9.4.6 Air Release Valve**

The air release valve on the discharge header shall be checked for free operation. Air release valves can stick in the open position, which will cause a visible spray of water. If the valve is stuck, clean the seat and check the float mechanism. At Ashcombe Works, the air release valve on the Low Lift discharge header has a history of sticking after the summer months due to a build-up of dried algae. This is a known issue and the valve is to be included in the monthly check without fail.

Section 4 – Treatment Works and Capacity

4.1 General

This section describes the principal treatment works operated by the Authority and the design parameters that govern their operation. It is intended as a reference for operational staff, maintenance planners, and engineers engaged in capital works. Where a particular parameter is subject to review, the review status is noted against the entry. All design figures quoted in this section are taken from the latest revision of the relevant process design memorandum, unless otherwise stated.

4.2 Eastgate Treatment Works (ENT02)

4.2.1 Location and Role

Eastgate Treatment Works is situated on the eastern edge of Thornwick, adjacent to the Eastgate Pumping Station and the main trunk road. The works receives raw water from the Eastgate Reservoir via a 600 mm diameter inlet main, and from the River Corby via the Corby Intake, which is approximately 1.2 km upstream of the works. The works provides the majority of the potable supply for District North and provides a top-up supply to District East during periods of high demand.

4.2.2 Design Capacity

Eastgate Treatment Works design capacity 45000 cubic metres per day. Record status: current. This figure is the current design capacity and is the basis for all hydraulic and process calculations within this manual. It represents the maximum sustainable output of the works under normal raw water quality conditions, with all process streams in service and no unit out of service for maintenance.

The design capacity is subject to annual review by the Engineering Planning Group. Any proposed change to the design capacity must be supported by a process modelling assessment and approved by the Head of Water Treatment before being incorporated into a future revision of this manual.

4.2.3 Process Description

The treatment process at Eastgate comprises the following principal stages, in order:

- Screening and grit removal (2 no. duty screens, 1 no. standby)
- Coagulation and flocculation (3 no. flocculation tanks, each with 2 no. stages)
- Clarification (4 no. lamella clarifiers)
- Rapid gravity filtration (8 no. filter beds, each with a nominal area of 45 m²)
- Chlorination (primary and secondary disinfection)
- pH correction and fluoridation
- Treated water storage (2 no. contact tanks, total capacity 12,500 m³)

The works operates as a conventional surface water treatment plant. The coagulation process uses ferric sulphate, with pH adjustment by lime. Polyelectrolyte is dosed as a flocculant aid. The normal coagulant dose range is 25–45 mg/l, depending on raw water turbidity and colour.

4.2.4 Flow Splitting and Control

Inlet flow is split equally between the three flocculation tanks by means of flow control valves on the inlet header. Each flocculation tank is fitted with a magnetic flow meter, and the flow set points are controlled by the works SCADA system. The normal operating range for each tank is 0.45–0.65 m³/s.

Clarified water from the lamella clarifiers is collected in a common clarified water channel, from which it is drawn by gravity to the filter inlet distribution chamber. The filter inlet is controlled by individual inlet valves, which are trimmed to give an equal flow to each filter bed. The normal filtration rate is 4.5–5.5 m/h, with a maximum rate of 6.0 m/h for short periods during filter backwash.

4.2.5 Filter Operation

Each rapid gravity filter bed is of the conventional downflow type, with a dual media of anthracite over sand, supported on a gravel layer and a nozzle floor. The normal filter run length is between 24 and 48 hours, depending on raw water quality. The end of a filter run is determined by the head loss across the bed, which is monitored continuously. The terminal head loss is normally 2.0 m, but this may be reduced to 1.5 m during periods of high algal activity in the raw water.

### 1. INTRODUCTION

#### 1.1 Purpose of this Manual

This manual sets out the approved methods, safety protocols, and performance standards for the operation and maintenance of the Thornwick Water Authority surface water treatment works. It is intended for use by all technicians, engineers, and operators engaged in the day-to-day running of the plant.

#### 1.2 Organisational Structure and Responsibilities

The treatment works operates under the overall management of the Operations Manager, who is responsible for the safe and efficient delivery of treated water to the distribution network. The operational team is structured as follows:

**Operations Manager** – Overall responsibility for plant performance, compliance with regulatory standards, staff management, and the annual review of this manual. The current Operations Manager is **Clarissa Finch**, who has held the post since **1 April 2019**. Clarissa Finch start date 2019-04-01 date. Record status: current. All significant operational decisions, emergency interventions, and deviations from standard procedures must be referred to the Operations Manager or, in their absence, to the Deputy Operations Manager.

**Deputy Operations Manager** – Supports the Operations Manager in the day-to-day running of the plant and assumes full responsibility in the absence of the Operations Manager. The post is currently held by **Dennis Okafor**. Responsibilities include shift rota management, coordination of maintenance activities with the workshop team, and the preparation of monthly performance reports.

**Senior Process Technician (Shift Leader)** – Each shift is led by a Senior Process Technician who directs the work of the process technicians on that shift. Shift Leaders are responsible for monitoring plant parameters, responding to alarms, and carrying out routine process checks. They report directly to the Deputy Operations Manager.

**Process Technicians** – Carry out routine operational duties including plant inspections, water quality sampling, filter backwashing, chemical dosing checks, and minor maintenance tasks. Process Technicians work on a rotating shift pattern covering 24 hours per day, 365 days per year.

**Maintenance Technicians (Mechanical and Electrical)** – Responsible for planned and reactive maintenance of all plant and equipment. Mechanical and electrical disciplines are separate, and each has its own supervisor. Maintenance activities are coordinated through the Works Maintenance Planner, who works closely with the Deputy Operations Manager.

**Water Quality Technicians** – Based in the on-site laboratory, they carry out the routine sampling and analysis programme. They also support the process team in investigating any water quality excursions and are responsible for the calibration of online analysers.

**Administrative Support** – The works office provides administrative support to the operations team, including the management of records, purchasing, and the coordination of training.

Section 1.5 Environmental Compliance and Permit Obligations

1.5.1 General Requirements

This Section sets out the environmental compliance requirements that apply to the operation and maintenance of Thornwick Water Authority (TWA) assets. All personnel involved in maintenance activities shall be familiar with the relevant permit conditions and shall conduct their work in a manner that prevents pollution and minimises environmental impact.

The principal environmental permit for TWA operations is held with the Environment Agency. The Environment Agency issued permit number WA-2018-0456. Record status: current. This permit is current and shall remain in force until such time as it is varied, transferred, or revoked by the Environment Agency. A copy of the permit and its associated conditions is held in the Environmental Compliance file in the Administrative Support office, and an electronic copy is available on the shared drive under TWA/Environmental/Permits.

1.5.2 Permit Conditions Summary

The following conditions are those most relevant to maintenance activities. This summary is not exhaustive. Where a conflict arises between this summary and the permit itself, the permit conditions shall take precedence.

- Discharges to watercourses shall not cause an obvious film, sheen, or discolouration on the surface of the water, nor cause the deposition of solids on the bed of the watercourse.
- Chemical storage areas shall be bunded to 110% of the capacity of the largest stored container, and all bunds shall be maintained free of accumulated rainwater and debris.
- Spill kits shall be available at all locations where oils, fuels, or chemicals are stored or used, and shall be checked monthly.
- Any incident that causes or has the potential to cause pollution shall be reported to the Environment Agency as soon as practicable, and in any event within 24 hours of the incident being detected.
- Maintenance activities that involve the use of concrete, cement, or grout shall be carried out in such a way as to prevent the entry of these materials into any drain or watercourse.

1.5.3 Reporting Obligations

The following reporting obligations apply to TWA under the permit:

- Annual environmental performance report, submitted to the Environment Agency by 31 January each year, covering the preceding calendar year.
- Quarterly notification of any permit breaches, submitted within 14 days of the end of each calendar quarter.
- Immediate notification by telephone of any incident that causes significant pollution, followed by a written report within 24 hours.

The Works Environmental Officer is responsible for preparing and submitting all reports required by the permit. In the absence of the Works Environmental Officer, the Operations Manager shall assume this responsibility.

1.5.4 Environmental Risk Assessment for Maintenance Activities

Before commencing any maintenance activity that could have an environmental impact, a site-specific environmental risk assessment shall be completed using Form TW/ERA/02. The risk assessment shall identify:

- The potential pathways by which pollutants could reach the environment;
- The likelihood and severity of any potential pollution event;
- The control measures required to prevent pollution;
- The spill response arrangements in place.

The completed form shall be kept with the work permit or work instruction for the activity, and shall be reviewed by the person in charge of the work before work commences.

1.5.5 Oil and Fuel Storage

All oil and fuel storage tanks on TWA sites shall be inspected weekly for signs of leakage, corrosion, or damage. The results of these inspections shall be recorded in the site log.

The frequencies set out below are the current controlled requirements. Any deviation from these frequencies requires written authorisation from the Operations Manager and must be recorded on Form TW/DEV/01.

The schedule is reviewed annually, or sooner if there is a change in legislation, a permit condition, or an incident that indicates a control is inadequate. Site managers are responsible for ensuring that the frequencies are met and that records are retained for a minimum of six years.

1.6.2 Regulatory Inspection Frequencies

The following frequencies apply to inspections required by external bodies. These are the current controlled values and are not to be altered without formal notification from the regulator concerned.

Drinking Water Inspectorate requires an inspection frequency of 12 months. Record status: current. The DWI inspection is a full audit of the treatment works, including raw water quality, treatment processes, disinfection, and distribution system integrity. The inspection is unannounced in principle, but TWA operates a standing invitation for DWI inspectors to attend at any reasonable time. The site log shall record the date of each DWI visit, the inspector's name, and the reference number of the inspection report.

1.6.3 Plant and Equipment Inspection Frequencies

All plant and equipment shall be inspected at the frequencies stated below. Where a fault is found during an inspection, the fault shall be logged on the maintenance system and a work order raised. Access to the SCADA system shall be controlled through individual user accounts. Each user shall be issued a unique username and password. Shared accounts are prohibited.

User roles and permissions:

| Role | Permissions |
|------|-------------|
| Operator | View displays, acknowledge alarms, acknowledge and reset trips, start/stop permitted plant |
| Senior Operator | All Operator permissions, plus editing set points within approved ranges, placing plant in manual |
| Technician | All Senior Operator permissions, plus forcing I/O points, editing control sequences |
| Engineer | All Technician permissions, plus configuration of displays, alarm set points, and user accounts |
| IT Systems Manager | All Engineer permissions, plus system administration, firmware updates, and database management |

Passwords shall be changed at least every 90 days. Accounts shall be locked after five unsuccessful login attempts. Access to the system from outside the operational network shall require a virtual private network (VPN) connection and two-factor authentication.

**1.7.6 Firmware Update Procedure**

Firmware updates to SCADA components shall be carried out in accordance with the change control procedure (Section 1.9). The following steps shall be followed:

1. Obtain the firmware update package from the equipment manufacturer or the IT Systems Manager.
2. Verify the integrity of the update package using the checksum provided by the manufacturer.
3. Back up the current configuration and database of the device to be updated.
4. Schedule the update during a planned outage or maintenance window. Updates to the primary server shall be carried out during a period of low operational demand, and shall be coordinated with the shift manager.
5. Apply the firmware update to the standby unit first. Verify that the standby unit operates correctly and can synchronise with the primary unit.
6. Once the standby unit is confirmed operational, apply the update to the primary unit.
7. After the update is complete, verify the system functionality, including alarm annunciation, data logging, and operator displays.
8. Record the update in the SCADA System Change Log, including the date, component, previous and new firmware versions, and the name of the person carrying out the update.

The current firmware status of the SCADA System is recorded in the SCADA System Configuration Register, held by the IT Systems Manager. The register shall be updated within one working day of any firmware change.

The SCADA System's last firmware update occurred on 2026-03-15. Record status: current. This update is the current controlled version in service as of the date of this manual revision. Any proposed update shall be assessed against the current version to determine the necessity and impact of the change.

**1.7.7 System Testing and Drills**

A full SCADA system failover test shall be carried out annually. The test shall simulate a failure of the primary server and verify that the standby server assumes control without loss of data. The test shall be witnessed by the IT Systems Manager and the Operations Manager, and the results shall be recorded in the SCADA System Change Log.

Quarterly, a communication path test shall be carried out on all RTUs. Each RTU shall be disconnected from the main communications network, and the fallback path shall be tested. RTUs that fail the test shall be reported to the IT Systems Manager.

**1.7.8 Known Limitations and Workarounds**

The following limitations are known and documented. These are not faults and shall not be logged as such unless the behaviour changes:

- The GUI for the Eastgate Depot standby workstation may display a delay of up to 5 seconds in refreshing process values during periods of high communications traffic. This is a known performance characteristic.

**Thornwick Water Authority Maintenance Manual**

**Section 1 – Safety**

**1.8 Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) Procedure**

**1.8.1 Purpose**

This procedure establishes the minimum requirements for the locking out and tagging of energy isolating devices whenever maintenance or servicing is carried out on plant or equipment where the unexpected energisation, start-up or release of stored energy could cause injury. All persons carrying out such work shall comply with this procedure. No person shall attempt to operate any switch, valve or other energy isolating device that has been locked or tagged out.

**1.8.2 Definitions**

For the purpose of this procedure:

- *Affected person* – a person whose work requires them to operate, or be in the vicinity of, equipment that is being serviced or maintained under a LOTO.
- *Authorised person* – a person who has been trained and authorised to carry out LOTO and to perform the servicing or maintenance.
- *Energy isolating device* – a mechanical device that physically prevents the transmission or release of energy, including manually operated circuit breakers, disconnect switches, line valves, and blocks.
- *Lockout* – the placement of a lock and tag on an energy isolating device in accordance with an established procedure, ensuring that the device cannot be operated until the lock is removed.
- *Tagout* – the placement of a tag on an energy isolating device in accordance with an established procedure, to indicate that the device may not be operated until the tag is removed. Tagout shall only be used where a device is not capable of being locked out, and shall always be used in conjunction with an additional safety measure, such as the removal of a fuse or the disconnection of a pipe.

**1.8.3 General Requirements**

1. LOTO shall be used whenever servicing or maintenance is carried out on plant or equipment that could be inadvertently energised, started, or release stored energy. This includes, but is not limited to, work on pumps, valves, actuators, chemical dosing systems, and electrical switchgear.
2. Only authorised persons shall carry out LOTO. A current list of authorised persons is held by the Operations Manager and displayed on the notice board at each depot.
3. Each authorised person shall be issued with a personal lock and key. Personal locks shall be uniquely keyed and shall only be operated by the person to whom they are issued. Keys shall not be duplicated or loaned.
4. Where more than one person is working on the same equipment, each person shall attach their own personal lock to the energy isolating device, or to a multi-lock hasp fitted to that device.
5. Locks and tags shall be of a robust construction and shall be capable of remaining in place for the duration of the work. Tags shall be weatherproof and shall be attached with a non-reusable cable tie or other secure fixing.
6. Tags shall be filled in legibly with a ballpoint pen or permanent marker, stating the reason for the lockout, the date, and the name of the authorised person. Do not use pencil or any other erasable medium.

**1.8.4 Procedure for Lockout/Tagout**

The following steps shall be carried out in the order given:

**1.8.5 Restoring Equipment to Service**

When the servicing or maintenance is complete, the following steps shall be carried out:

1. **Inspect.** The authorised person shall inspect the work area to ensure that all tools and materials have been removed, and that guards and safety devices have been replaced.
2. **Notify.** The authorised person shall notify all affected persons that the equipment is to be returned to service.
3. **Remove.** Each lock and tag shall be removed by the authorised person who applied it. Where a lock cannot be removed by the person who applied it, the procedure in Section 1.8.6 shall be followed.
4. **Energise.** After all locks and tags have been removed, the equipment shall be returned to service using the normal starting procedure.

**THORNWICK WATER AUTHORITY**
**MAINTENANCE MANUAL**

**Section 9 – Preventive Maintenance Schedules and Lubrication**

---

**9.1 General**

This section sets out the routine preventive maintenance tasks, lubrication schedules, and inspection routines for the plant and network assets owned and operated by the Authority. The schedules are to be followed in conjunction with the specific asset records held at each depot and the manufacturer’s published instructions. Where a conflict exists between this manual and the manufacturer’s instructions, the more stringent requirement shall apply.

Preventive maintenance is to be recorded on the appropriate job card or, where electronic recording is in use, in the asset management system. All work is to be signed and dated by the technician carrying out the task. Supervisors shall review completed records on a weekly basis to confirm that the schedules are being met.

**9.2 Scheduling Conventions**

The following conventions apply to the schedules in this section:

| Abbreviation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| W | Weekly |
| M | Monthly |
| Q | Quarterly (every 3 months) |
| SA | Six-monthly (every 6 months) |
| A | Annually |
| 2Y | Two-yearly |
| h | Running hours (cumulative since last overhaul) |

Schedules are based on a 52-week year. Where a task falls due during a shut-down or outage, it shall be brought forward and completed during that outage where practicable. Tasks may be deferred by no more than 10% of the interval, subject to the approval of the Operations Manager. Deferrals are to be noted on the job card.

**9.3 Pumps – General Purpose (Centrifugal)**

The following schedule applies to all centrifugal pumps in the raw water, treated water, and sludge handling duty, with the exception of the borehole pumps covered under Section 9.4.

| Task | Interval | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| Check gland leakage; adjust or repack as necessary | W | 9.3.1 |
| Check bearing housing temperature by hand; record any reading above 70°C | W | 9.3.2 |
| Check for unusual noise or vibration | W | 9.3.3 |
| Check coupling alignment using straight edge and feeler gauge | Q | 9.3.4 |
| Lubricate bearings (grease) – see Section 9.8 | Q | 9.8.2 |
| Check and tighten foundation bolts | SA | 9.3.5 |
| Check flexible coupling elements for wear; replace if cracked or perished | SA | 9.3.6 |
| Inspect impeller and wear rings; measure clearances and record | A | 9.3.7 |
| Check shaft run-out at coupling and at gland | A | 9.3.8 |
| Megger test motor windings (in conjunction with electrical section) | A | 9.3.9 |
| Overhaul – replace bearings, mechanical seal or gland packing, and inspect all internal surfaces | 20,000 h | 9.3.10 |

**9.3.1 Gland Leakage**

For packed glands, the acceptable leakage rate is a steady drip of between 10 and 30 drops per minute when the pump is running at its duty point. A dry gland indicates that the packing is too tight, which will cause scoring of the shaft sleeve. A stream of water indicates that the packing is too loose or is worn. Adjust the gland nuts by a quarter turn at a time and re-check after 15 minutes of running.

For mechanical seals, there should be no visible leakage. A small amount of weeping may occur during the initial run-in period of a new seal and is acceptable for the first 4 hours of operation. Thereafter, any leakage is a fault and the seal shall be replaced.

**9.3.2 Bearing Housing Temperature**

The bearing housing temperature shall be checked by hand. If the housing is too hot to hold the back of a hand against for more than 3 seconds, the temperature is likely to be above 70°C and the pump shall be taken out of service for investigation. The pump shall not be returned to service until the cause of the overheating has been identified and rectified. Record the temperature and the action taken on the job card.

**Thornwick Water Authority Maintenance Manual**

**Section 9.4 – Routine Inspection of Horizontal Split-Case Pumps**

The checks in this section apply to the horizontal split-case pumps installed at Crowthorne Hill Pumping Station (CHPS), Merrow Lane Booster (MLB), and the Low Lift station at Ashcombe Works. They supplement the general pump checks in Section 9.3 and are to be carried out in accordance with the frequency table below.

| Item | Frequency | Ref. |
|---|---|---|
| Check suction and discharge pressure gauges for erratic readings | W | 9.4.1 |
| Inspect coupling guard for security and correct alignment | W | 9.4.2 |
| Check drain valve at bottom of casing is closed and not weeping | W | 9.4.3 |
| Check casing joint for signs of leakage; note any seepage on job card | W | 9.4.4 |
| Verify pressure switch settings against pump curve for the current duty | M | 9.4.5 |
| Check air release valve operation on the discharge header | M | 9.4.6 |
| Inspect baseplate and grout for cracks or fretting | SA | 9.4.7 |
| Check shaft sleeve condition at gland area; measure and record wear | A | 9.4.8 |
| Dismantle and inspect non-return valve on discharge; renew if flap worn | A | 9.4.9 |

**9.4.1 Pressure Gauge Readings**

Erratic gauge readings usually indicate air entrainment or a partially blocked suction strainer. If the suction gauge shows a vacuum higher than the value on the duty card, stop the pump and check the strainer. Do not attempt to clear a blocked strainer by throttling the discharge valve. Record the readings on the daily log sheet at CHPS. At MLB, where the suction head is positive, a sudden drop in suction pressure may indicate a fault with the town’s inlet main; contact the Network Controller before taking the pump out of service.

**9.4.2 Coupling Guard**

The guard shall be in place at all times when the pump is running. Check that all fixing bolts are present and that the guard does not rub on the coupling. If the guard has been removed for maintenance, it shall be replaced before the pump is returned to service. A missing guard is a reportable safety defect and shall be entered on the safety observation register.

**9.4.3 Casing Drain Valve**

The drain valve at the bottom of the casing shall be closed except when the pump is being drained. If the valve is found weeping, tighten the gland nut. If weeping continues, replace the valve. Do not leave a bucket under the valve as a permanent arrangement; this is not an acceptable long-term fix.

**9.4.4 Casing Joint Leakage**

A small amount of seepage at the casing joint can occur on older pumps and is not necessarily a fault. Wipe the joint clean and monitor. If the seepage increases or becomes a steady drip, the joint shall be re-sealed at the next available outage. For CHPS Pump 1, a previous seepage at the top half of the casing was traced to a distorted joint face. That pump is booked for a full overhaul in the current financial year and the joint faces will be machined true at that time.

**9.4.5 Pressure Switch Settings**

Pressure switch settings shall be checked against the current duty card for the pump. The duty card is held in the pump house at CHPS and in the kiosk at MLB. Settings shall be verified using a calibrated test gauge. Do not adjust settings without reference to the duty card. If a setting is found to be outside the permitted band, record the discrepancy on the job card and notify the Mechanical Engineer.

**9.4.6 Air Release Valve**

The air release valve on the discharge header shall be checked for free operation. Air release valves can stick in the open position, which will cause a visible spray of water. If the valve is stuck, clean the seat and check the float mechanism. At Ashcombe Works, the air release valve on the Low Lift discharge header has a history of sticking after the summer months due to a build-up of dried algae. This is a known issue and the valve is to be included in the monthly check without fail.
